title: Fufu
author: Akosua Mensah
desc: Cassava and green plantain boiled to fork-tender and pounded in a mortar — the plantain first, then the cassava, then the two together.
longDesc: Fufu is the swallow the forest zone is built on, and it is pounded rather than stirred. Cassava and green plantain are peeled, the cassava core and the plantain seeds removed, boiled about thirty minutes until fork-tender, then pounded — plantain to a smooth dough first, cassava after, the two brought together and moulded into a ball. The technical literature is clearer than the recipes about what you are aiming for: the boiled starch must be pulverised into a wet powdery form before it binds itself into fufu. No named source publishes weights, pounding times or a pounding cue, and that gap is stated rather than filled.
ingredients: Water, enough to just cover the cassava and plantain
equipment: Bowl of water, for wetting the hands
steps: Peel and slice the cassava and plantain, removing the cassava core and the plantain seeds.
Cover with water and cook over medium heat 30 minutes, until fork-tender.
Pound the plantain first, to a smooth dough.
Combine the two and pound together until the mass binds into itself and pulls away clean.
Wet your hands and mould into a smooth ball.
Serve in a bowl with soup poured around it (GHA011).
chefTips: Fork-tender is the boiling cue, and it is the only one published. Undercooked cassava will not pulverise and you will pound forever.
Plantain first, cassava second, then together. Pounding them from the start gives an uneven mass.

The technique cue worth knowing, from a KNUST engineering paper on mechanising the job: the boiled starch must be pulverised into a wet powdery form BEFORE it binds itself into fufu. If you are pounding a lump rather than breaking it down, you are too early.
Wet hands, not oiled. Water stops it sticking without changing the surface.
Raw cassava contains toxins, so it is never tasted raw and never undercooked — the source says so plainly.
Fufu is not chewed. It is pinched off, dipped in soup and swallowed, which is why the texture matters more than the flavour.
No source gives weights, a pounding time or a pounding cue. The ratio above is one tuber to two plantain fingers as printed; adjust toward more plantain for a softer ball.
commonMistakes: Boiling until soft rather than fork-tender, which gives a wet, slack fufu.
Leaving the woody cassava core in.
Pounding both starches together from the start.
Serving it in pieces to be chewed rather than as a ball to be pinched and swallowed.
sources: Quantities and method adapted from 'Fufu Recipe', byline as printed 'Imma Adamu', africanbites.com, 13 April 2026. Yield as printed: 4 servings. BYLINE FLAG: the site is branded Immaculate Bites / African Bites and its owner is believed — unverified — to be Immaculate Ogu, so the printed byline name could not be reconciled with the site's ownership. Recorded as printed with that caveat. ATTRIBUTION FLAG: the page attributes the dish only to 'West African cuisine', not to Ghana or to the Akan. The Akan attribution here comes from the Osseo-Asare and CSIR sources below, not from this page.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 1 medium cassava tuber; 2 fingers green plantain; Water (enough to just cover the cassava and plantain); 1 teaspoon salt (optional). Method as printed: peel and slice cassava and plantain, removing the cassava core and plantain seeds; cover with water and cook over medium heat 30 minutes; traditional method pounds plantain to a smooth dough, then pounds cassava, combines and moulds. DONENESS CUE as printed: 'fork-tender'. WARNING as printed: 'Raw cassava contains toxins that can make you sick.'
QUANTITY GAP, stated rather than filled: the only measure is 'one medium tuber' with no weight, and NO POUNDING TIME appears anywhere on the page.

THE POUNDING TECHNIQUE CUE, and the most useful single sentence found on fufu anywhere: Kessey K.O., Dadoo R.E., Ansong L.E., 'Towards Mechanisation of Fufu Pounding', Journal of Science and Technology (KNUST) 18(2), 1998 — abstract only. Verbatim: 'For best results, the boiled carbohydrate must be pulverised into a wet powdery form before binding itself into Fufu.' The abstract adds that machines 'have not been fully successful in producing Fufu in the right plasticity and consistency as desired by Ghanaians.' It gives no ratios or times.

CULTURAL CONTEXT from Fran Osseo-Asare, "'We Eat First With Our Eyes': On Ghanaian Cuisine", Gastronomica, Winter 2002, byline as printed 'By Fran Osseo-Asare'. Verbatim: 'To prepare fufu, Ghanaians use a variety of starches alone or in combination (yam, cassava, green plantain, and cocoyam, a.k.a. taro)'. And: 'The fufu softens the sound as the pestle hits the mortar with a soothing thumping as women prepare dinner.' And: 'Fufu is is not chewed, but swallowed whole…' — the doubled 'is' is as printed. Context only; no quantities.

ON THE STARCH COMBINATION, from Tortoe C., Johnson P-N.T., Oduro-Yeboah C., Anaglo J., Quayson E.T., CSIR Food Research Institute, Accra, 2006: 'Pounded fufu is prepared by pounding boiled cassava with plantain, yam or cocoyam depending on the location of the consumers and access to the staple.' NOTE: the text extraction rendered this as 'Pounded Juju', which is an OCR or extraction error and is corrected here only in that one word. A date flag on that report: it describes training on '30th March and 5th July 2006' under a single 2006 date.

THE REAL GAP, named: there is NO acceptable written traditional pounding recipe with weights, times or a pounding cue in any source consulted. The KNUST abstract is the only technique cue found. Oduro-Yeboah, Johnson, Sakyi-Dawson, Abbey, 'Instrumental and Sensory Texture Profile Attributes of Fufu from Cassava-Plantain Flour', J. Root Crops 33(1):53-56, 2007 was checked and its abstract gives no ratios either.

NOT USED: an 'Africa News Cookbook' compilation hosted at africa.upenn.edu gives a fufu of 2½ cups Bisquick, 2½ cups instant potato flakes and 6 cups water, stirred 10-15 minutes. That is an American pantry substitute rather than fufu and is recorded as such, not as a version of this dish.

A TOOL CAVEAT ON THIS WHOLE COLLECTION, stated once here: the pages behind these entries were read through a fetch tool that returns model-summarised text rather than raw page source. Quantities were re-requested verbatim on a second pass wherever possible and only consistent figures were carried through. Where a figure survived only one pass it is marked in that recipe's sources.
storage: Best eaten at once. It stiffens and cracks within a few hours and does not refrigerate well.
reheating: Not recommended. Fufu is made to order.
healthBenefits: Green plantain is high in resistant starch, which ferments in the colon rather than spiking blood sugar.
Cassava supplies vitamin C and manganese.
No oil, salt or sugar beyond the optional teaspoon.
culturalNote: The sound of fufu being pounded at dusk is one of the recognisable sounds of a Ghanaian town, and Osseo-Asare's line about the pestle thumping into the mortar is the best description of it in print. It is eaten with the right hand, pinched off, dipped and swallowed without chewing — a texture-led food in which a lump or a sour note is immediately obvious.
